newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW-GERMAN ECONOMISTS' COMMENT.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW-GERMAN ECONOMISTS' COMMENT.

text.p: Following are comments from Frankfurt-based economists after a runoff vote in France's parliamentary election pointing to a victory for the left.
THOMAS MAYER, ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS.

In both countries, Germany and France, fiscal consolidation and austerity is going to be very difficult. In Germany we have the gold row and right now there is an emergency meeting about the 1998 budget. Fiscal austerity is politically very hard to enact.
The message out of France is that the French electorate is also resisting stronger fiscal austerity. But there is also some relief that the pro-EMU faction won.

We probably cannot count on as much fiscal consolidation and tightening as just a few months ago and this is not very good news for European bond markets which were counting on significant consolidation.

The risks for EMU have increased somewhat but I still don't believe that the EMU process is going to be derailed. Remember it was the Socialists who negotiated the Maastricht treaty. But the risks are higher before all these events.
The main message is that monetary union will not be based on tight fiscal policy. Normally the response to looser fiscal policy is tighter monetary policy.
If monetary policy accomodates looser fiscal policy then the euro will be a weaker currency but if monetary policy resists, the euro will be strong.

Obviously a year and a half is a long time in politics and it would be misguided to try to make a judgement now, but having said this, the Social Democratic (SPD) Party well feel very reassured by the French left because the French left is an old fashioned left-wing party that is playing with economic ideas from the 1970s. The SPD is also an old fashioned left wing party.
They will get more reassurance from this than from what happened in the United Kingdom because Labour is not an old fashioned party.
ECKHARD SCHULTE, ECONOMIST, IBJ
It's looking as if the conservative era is coming to an end.
I think many people in Germany will now discuss the euro much more intensively than they have done so far.
The most important question from the German point of view is, is France still a partner to execute monetary union?

We have to wait and see what programme the Socialists come up with. I do not doubt the Socialists will go into the euro but probably not with (a budget deficit of) 3.0 percent (of gross domestic product) and probably not with a core euro (narrow membership). That is the decisive question. I think they still will follow EMU, but they would like to fudge the criteria.
The majority of voters decided to elect a party which favours a fudge and a broad EMU. It's now fudge or delay. The ball is in the German camp.
(much depends on outcome of crisis talks at Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office on Sunday on budget and gold row)
It's going to be a very hard time for the (German government) coalition.

If we see the end of the coalition very soon, it's probably more likely we can give in to a broad EMU. If Kohl survives, there is a good chance it (EMU) will be delayed. Kohl knows (a broad EMU) would be the end of his political career. He cannot make a broad EMU acceptable to the German population.
If there is a new constellation (of political parties) in the next few months that is a different story.
JOACHIM FELS, MORGAN STANLEY

There's sense of relief that the Socialists will be able to form a government without relying on the Communists. The perception is that a Socialist government that had to rely on the Communists would be less likely to take the fiscal measures necessary to qualify for EMU.
We saw little difference between the Socialists and a centre-right government led by (National Assembly speaker Philippe) Seguin.
I don't think the markets will react violently here. The prospects for a Socialist victory were priced in last week. I even see room for some improvement.
(on whether controversy over the German government's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves would embolden French Socialists to seek wider renegotiations)

The Socialists will certainly be watching what is going on in Germany, but I think the row between the government and the Bundesbank is seen as evidence of the governments' determination to mee the magic three percent number.
